turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Well, I have currently 26 strategies to be funny. Some are better for business than others. I will give you two that we can use in business all the time. The first one you can use is nostalgia, because nostalgia is always funny. The fact that the first VCR I had was 22 pounds and had a remote control attached by a cord that was thick enough that I could trip my brother as he walked through the living room is funny. The fact that I grew up and no one was allergic to anything and we all ate bread, packed with gluten and baked in asbestos factories and no one ever wore a helmet while they rode their bike. All of these things can be made to be funny. And it's so easy in business because oftentimes you are rolling out a new product or a new service or you're updating a product or service in a way that allows you to speak nostalgically about the past. (00:54:09): I was working with this company and they failed me. They did not listen to my advice which was a mistake. They're like an Indeed company. They're helping find employees for companies they're one of these people. And I wanted to start their narrative with the idea of in 1983, the primary source of employment was a 16-year- old kid riding on the back of a Schwinn, throwing newspapers at doors. And in that newspaper, which was like a paper version of the internet, you would turn to the back page and on that page there was the help wanted ads. And that was essentially all you had to find a job in 1983. Everything was geographically based, meaning you only could look into three or four towns around you to find a job. And it had to be in the paper and you had to own a phone connected to a wall so you could call a company within business hours and hope to get an interview. (00:55:03): All of the power lived with the employers in 1983 and a 16-year-old who was dropping a newspaper off at your porch every day. That's funny. Again, I didn't even try to be funny with it. I just stated the facts. We could have punched that up and made it really funny. And then we flip the script again, the opposites in story. In the beginning, employers had all the power. Today, employees have all the power. Because today you can work in Singapore or Chattanooga, while you're living in Orlando. And today you don't have to wait for a 16-year-old to deliver the paper with all of your job opportunities. Every single job opportunity on the planet is now accessible to you on the internet. And you can work basically anywhere from anywhere. So that's why we need companies like Indeed or the company I was working for, because they have to actually gain some power for the employers. (00:55:57): So that was the narrative we were going to tell, and the beginning would've been funny. And the CEO of the company said, "I don't like it." He said, "Nobody cares about the 1980s." Which was the dumbest thing he could have said because Stranger Things was the biggest television show on television at the time, which was nothing. But in 1980s. And if he just looked around, he would see that 1980s fashion is coming back. 1980s music is being popularized again. We're remaking 1980s music all the time. Taylor Swift put out an album called 1989. Whether or not the 1980s are relevant or not, it's relevant to talk about the past as a company to demonstrate your expertise in your field. To understand that we know the market backwards and forwards for the last 50 years. We have expertise and we can demonstrate it by telling a story. So that's the power of nostalgia and we can use that all the time in business to make people laugh. (00:56:50): The other one I'll give you, again, there's a whole bunch, but a simple one is a game they used to play on Sesame Street, which is one of these things that's not like the other. Essentially it's three things. Two of them are expected and one is unexpected, and the unexpected one will be funny. So you can say like, well, my competitor, they have this. My hardware competitor, the guy down the street, he does sell shovels just like I do. That's true. And he does offer a wide selection of nails just like I do. But there's a nameless, faceless machine at the front of the store that you have to swipe your own stuff through and your credit card, there's not actually a human being in the store. And we can make that funny by showing that the third one is unlike the other two. So it's essentially a simple game once I've told it to you, you'll see every comic do it all the time. They just say thing that's expected, thing that's expected, unexpected thing, and you make it funny. So it's a simple trick that we use in business all the time.
turns.zh:
嗯，我目前有26种制造幽默的策略。有些策略更适合商业场合。我会给你们两个在商业中随时都能用的技巧。第一个策略是利用怀旧情怀，因为怀旧总是很有趣。比如我记得自己第一个录像机重达22磅，遥控器的线缆粗得能绊倒在客厅里走路的兄弟；再比如我成长的那个年代，所有人都不对任何东西过敏，我们都吃着含麸质、在石棉工厂烘焙的面包长大；还有大家骑自行车时从不戴头盔。这些童年趣事都能被转化为笑料。在商业中运用起来也很简单，因为你经常要推出新产品、新服务，或者对现有产品进行升级，这时候就可以用怀旧的叙事方式来回顾往昔。（00:54:09）：我曾和一家公司合作，他们让我失望了。他们不听取我的建议，这真是个错误。这家公司类似Indeed这样的平台，帮企业招人，自己也是其中一员。我想用1983年的故事来开场，当时找工作的主要渠道是16岁的孩子骑着施文自行车递送报纸。报纸就像早期的互联网版块，人们翻到最后一页就能看到招聘广告。1983年找工作全凭地理位置限制，只能在周边三四个城镇寻找机会，还得在办公时间用固定电话联系公司，祈求能获得面试机会。（00:55:03）：1983年所有权力都掌握在雇主手中，16岁的报童每天送报上门。这种对比很搞笑。我甚至没刻意幽默，只是陈述事实。我们本可以把故事推向高潮，但又反转了叙事逻辑。过去雇主掌握主动权，如今员工则占据上风。如今你可以在新加坡或查塔努加工作，而住在奥兰多。互联网让全球就业机会触手可及，你可以在任何地方开展业务。这就是为什么我们需要Indeed这样的公司，因为它们要为雇主争取主动权。（00:55:57）：这原本是个精彩的故事开局，但客户说"我不喜欢这个创意"，还说"没人对80年代感兴趣"。这是最愚蠢的反应，毕竟《怪奇物语》当时可是最火的剧集。80年代元素正卷土重来，80年代音乐重获人气，我们不断翻拍80年代经典。泰勒·斯威夫特甚至出专辑《1989》。无论80年代是否过时，以往经历都能证明你对行业的深刻洞察。通过讲述故事展示专业度，让客户明白你对过去50年市场了如指掌，专业素养无可置疑。这就是怀旧的力量，我们在商业中随时都能用它逗人开怀。
（00:56:50）：另外一个例子我再给你们讲一下，类似的例子有很多，但最简单的一个就是《芝麻街》里常玩的游戏——找出与众不同的事物。核心在于呈现三个物品，其中两个是常见的，一个是出乎意料的，而出乎意料的部分要足够有趣。比如你可以说：我的竞争对手，他们也有这个产品。我的五金店竞争对手，就在街对面，他和我一样卖铲子。没错，他也和我一样提供种类繁多的钉子。但他店里有个无名无牌的机器，顾客需要自己扫描商品和信用卡，店里根本没有真人服务员。我们可以通过强调第三个元素与前两个的不同来制造笑点。所以一旦我把这个游戏规则讲清楚，你们就会发现每个喜剧演员都会用这个套路。他们先说出预期中的事物，再说出预期中的事物，最后说出出乎意料的部分，然后把它变得搞笑。这是我们在商业中常用的简单技巧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is awesome. This list you're talking about, is this going to be in your new book that you're writing?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到的这个清单，会写进你正在创作的新书里吗？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Not all 26 of them because some are not the best business ones in the world, but a large number of them. I think I maybe have the top 12 that work best in business in terms of humor. But you can just take a humor class. I teach humor all the time. I teach all 26 strategies. It's something that can be practiced. The beautiful thing is so often many of the strategies that I offer in business, if it doesn't end up being funny, you're still telling a story. It's not a ba-bum-bum-ching joke. We're not telling those jokes. We're telling humor in the confines of a story so that if this joke doesn't land we're still telling a story. And oftentimes people don't even realize we were trying to be funny.
turns.zh: 不一定是全部26个策略，因为有些并非商业场景下最有效的幽默方式，但其中有很多实用例子。我认为在商业语境中，最具效果的幽默策略或许有前12个。不过你完全可以去上幽默课程啊。我常年教授幽默技巧，涵盖全部26种策略。这是可以通过刻意练习提升的能力。关键在于，许多我在商业场合提到的幽默策略，即便最终没能引发笑点，至少能让故事更连贯。毕竟我们讲的不是那种“一语惊人”的笑话，而是将幽默元素融入故事架构中。所以即便某个笑点没能成功，整个叙事依然能保持趣味性，而听众往往意识不到我们在刻意制造笑点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to come back to where story can help you in your work. So obviously giving a public talk is the classic way to use this, maybe giving a PowerPoint deck in a meeting. Is there any other maybe non-obvious places that you think this skill can help you in that's not just like, "Hey everyone welcome to my..."
turns.zh: 接下来我要讲讲故事思维在职场中的应用。公开演讲和会议中的PPT演示都是典型应用场景，但还有哪些不那么显而易见的场景能受益于这种技巧呢？比如不只是开场白“大家好，欢迎来到我的……”

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Well, I've worked with a lot of scientists in biotech and places like that. I worked with a biotech company. Five of their scientists were going to a conference. And essentially it's a company that sells tubes. All of their competitors sell a tube for experiments and you have to retrofit the tube to fit your needs. The company I was working with, they sell 12 different versions of the tube. Better sized so you don't have to retrofit it, much more expensive, but the reliability of your experiments are improved by using their properly sized tubes. So I prepare all the scientists and they all do a good job. They all tell stories of some sort and they go off to their conference. (00:59:43): One guy though doesn't present any data whatsoever. He just tells a story. He tells a story about going to the grocery store and when he goes to the grocery store, his family is really annoying when it comes to apples. Because everyone likes a different apple. So he's got to go and he is got to buy three Honeycrisp for his wife and two Gala for his daughter. And they're baking a pie this week so they got to get some McIntosh and he likes Red Delicious. He said, "It's a nightmare buying these apples." So he tells that story about the nightmare of buying apples, and then he says, "That's what my company does." There are companies that say, "We offer McIntosh, make do with it. You're going to make your pies, you're, you're going to eat it. All of the things that you want to do with an apple, all you get is McIntosh. Good luck. We believe you should have access to all the apples. We believe that you have particular needs and specific requirements, and we're going to make sure you have it. Just like my family gets all the apples they want. (01:00:42): It's all he said. A longer version of it, but that's it. No data. He got more leads at the conference than the other four scientists combined. Now the vice president of marketing was not happy about this at all when I met I met with her. Because she's a scientist. She's 50 years old. For her entire life, she's been sending scientists to conferences and presenting data. And she said to me, "So what am I going to do? Send scientists to conferences now and not present data?" And I said, "Well, I mean maybe because it worked" And she said, "Well, what about the data?" I said, "Now that he has the leads, you don't think they're going to want the data?" He's going to get on the phone and they're going to say, tell us about the data. But now they've established a connection. (01:01:22): And the best thing about that story, the thing she didn't even understand was, every single time someone at that conference goes into a grocery store now and they're looking at apples, they're going to think about that company. And it's a positive feeling that they're going to have about that company. If they have forgotten to call, but they meant to call, when they're picking out a Honeycrisp at the grocery store, they're going to make a note. Oh, right, I got to call that company and look into the tubes that they sell. We create positive connections with items in the world related to our company by telling stories, and that means we've built advertising into people's lives without them even being aware that we've done it. So there's a billion ways to add storytelling into business. It's just another one.
turns.zh: 嗯，我在生物科技公司和类似领域与很多科学家共事过。我曾在一家生物科技公司工作。他们公司的五位科学家要去参加一个会议。这家公司主要销售实验用试管，但所有竞争对手都只能卖标准尺寸的试管，用户还得自己改装才能满足需求。而我合作的这家公司，生产了12种不同规格的试管，尺寸更精准，省去了改装步骤，虽然价格更贵，但实验的可靠性显著提升。于是我帮所有科学家做了准备，他们都表现出色。会议上每个人都分享了自己的故事，然后各自离场。（00:59:43）不过有个人根本没展示任何数据，只讲了一个故事。他讲的是去超市买苹果的经历，家人总爱挑剔不同品种，导致他要为妻子买三个Honeycrisp苹果，为女儿买两个Gala苹果。这周要烤派，所以还得买些McIntosh苹果，而他自己偏爱Red Delicious。他感叹“买苹果真是件头疼事”。接着他说这就是我们公司的理念。有些公司会说：“有McIntosh就将就吧，反正你又要做派、吃苹果，我们只提供通用型号。”但我们相信客户应该拥有全套选择。我们深知每个客户有特定需求，必须满足他们的个性化要求，就像我家人能随心所欲挑选苹果一样。（01:00:42）这就是他整个演讲内容。虽然版本更长，但核心就是这些。没有数据。他在会议上收获的潜在客户，比其他四位科学家加起来还要多。营销副总裁听完后非常不满，毕竟她也是科学家，50岁了，一生都在带科学家参会展示数据。她质问：“那我现在该怎么办？带科学家去参会却不展示数据？”我说：“既然有效，为什么不继续？”她又问：“那数据呢？”我说：“现在他有潜在客户了，难道你不觉得他们会想要数据吗？他们会打电话问数据的。但现在你们已经建立了联系。”（01:01:22）最妙的是，她根本没意识到这件事的重要性。现在每次参会者去超市选苹果时，都会想起这家公司。这会给他们留下积极印象。即使他们忘记打电话，但在超市挑Honeycrisp苹果时，心里会记下：“哦，对了，得联系那家公司看看他们卖的试管。”我们通过讲故事，在与公司相关的事物中建立积极联结，让广告潜移默化地融入人们的生活。商界可以通过讲故事创造无数可能性，这只是其中一种。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on this two-way approach. One is, you have a problem. Let me think of a story to help me solve this problem, versus I'm going to become a storyteller, come up with this whole brick wall of stories and then I'll deploy them. You said that the first approach is not something you'd recommend. I imagine most people are probably going to be in that bucket like I don't want to be a storyteller. I just want to solve my problems and stories can sometimes help me there. So maybe in that bucket, do you have any advice for how to find a story that somehow helps you with that problem on demand, or is it just like that is not going to work? You're not going to think of a story every time you have some problem?
turns.zh: 你提到了这种双向方法。一种是，当你遇到问题时，先想办法找到一个能帮助自己解决问题的故事，而不是一开始就想成为一个讲故事的人，先编造一堆故事然后再去应用它们。你说第一种方法不值得推荐。我想大多数人可能都会持同样的态度，就是不想成为讲故事的人，只想解决自己的问题，而故事有时能帮到我们。那么对于这种情况，你有没有什么建议，能让人们在需要时随手就能找到一个有助于解决问题的故事，还是说这根本行不通？每次遇到问题都得临时想出一个故事？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: I think sometimes you will. I have a company that calls me metaphor man. They call me essentially and say-
turns.zh: 我觉得有时候还是能做到的。我有一家公司，他们叫我“比喻达人”。他们基本上会打电话给我，说——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I get that.
turns.zh: 我懂了。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: "... we've added a boring feature to our boring platform and we need to make people understand what it does. Will you give us the metaphor we need?" They don't understand that I'm not really generating metaphors. I am just taking stories from my life, pulling myself out of the story. And if you take yourself out of a story, often what's left is a metaphor, a simile, an example. And then I just offer that to them. And I tell them, if you just use some of my storytelling generating techniques, you could do the same thing. But they're a bandaid company. They just want me to fix things. And I understand that. If you're trying to do it, the best way to tell a story about something that you want people to understand is to do what I call speaking with adjacency, which means we're not going to match content to content. Instead, we're going to match theme, meaning or message. (01:03:33): So that scientist, for example, he wasn't talking about tubes. He was talking about how people deserve to get what they want in life. His family deserves to get the apples they want, and you as a business deserves to get the tubes that you want. But so often in business what people think is content to content, well, I got to find a way to talk about these tubes to make people understand how important they are. And I say, well, let's not talk about the tubes. Let's talk about something else instead, and then we're going to move what we were talking about over two tubes. We are going to snap it in place. That snap when someone realizes, you were telling me about apples, but really you were telling me about tubes. That snap is so powerful. I use it with students all the time. (01:04:21): A student acts like a fool, gets in trouble sitting at my desk. I'm not talking about their behavior. I'm telling a story that they have no idea why I am telling them the story. They're like, "I'm in trouble. Why is he telling me about his dog? Why is he telling me a story about his dog when he was 12?" Because I'm going to snap it into place. Because I'm not talking about content, theme, meaning or message. So when they come to me and they say, "Here's what we've got." I'm not thinking about the thing. I'm thinking about, what is the theme they want to convey or the meaning that they want to convey or the message they want to convey. And what story do I have that will match that or what story can I get out of them? (01:04:58): The scientist did not come to me with the apple story. The scientist came to me with the tubes and I said, "Well, it sounds like you're a company that wants to give people what they need. Let's find a story in your life about a time when you have to give people something that they need." And we brainstormed it. And when we landed on apples, I knew we had it. Because he was going to be able to talk about, I'm a father. I'm a husband. I'm the husband who takes apple orders from his family before going to the grocery store. I'm going to be able to be funny, because befuddled husbands in grocery stores are always funny. So it wasn't that he came to me with a story. I came to him with the idea of let's look at theme, meaning and message and then snap it over to the tubes. That's what we want to do when we're putting a band-aid on. We don't want to think about what we're talking about. We want to think about the feelings we want people to have about what we're talking about.
turns.zh: 他们不明白，我并非在创造隐喻。我只是从自己生活中的故事中汲取灵感，将自己抽离出故事框架。若你能抽离出故事，剩下的往往就是隐喻、明喻或示例。然后我把这些呈现给他们，并告诉他们，只要运用我教授的讲故事技巧，他们也能做到同样的事。但他们是一家急于解决问题的公司，只想让我快速修补现状。我理解这种心理。若你想讲述一个能让听众理解某事的故事，最好的方法是采用我所谓的“邻近性讲述法”——即不刻意对应内容，而是匹配主题、含义或传达的信息。（01:03:33）举个例子，那位科学家讲的并非试管，他讲的是人们理应得到想要的东西。他的家人理应得到想要的苹果，而作为企业的你们也理应得到想要的试管。但商业界常把内容对接视为唯一解决之道。我要告诉你们，关键在于用邻近性思维将主题、含义或信息巧妙衔接。比如那位科学家讲的不是试管，而是人们理应得到想要的东西。他的家人理应得到想要的苹果，而作为企业的你们也理应得到想要的试管。（01:04:21）有个学生表现得愚钝，在我办公桌前惹上麻烦。我讲的不是他的行为，而是讲述一个他完全不明白我为何讲述的故事。他们会问：“我有麻烦了，他为什么讲自己12岁养狗的故事？”因为我要让故事与主题契合。我不关注内容，而是关注他们想要传达的主题、含义或信息，以及我能从他们那里挖掘出的故事。（01:04:58）那位科学家来找我时讲的不是苹果故事，而是试管。我说：“听起来你们公司想为人们提供所需。让我们从你的生活寻找一个必须为他人提供所需的时刻。”我们头脑风暴后，确定了苹果这个主题。因为他能讲述：我是父亲、丈夫，负责在去超市前收集家人的苹果订单。我还能制造笑料，因为在超市里手足无措的丈夫总是很搞笑。所以这不是他带着故事来找我，而是我引导他关注主题、含义和信息，然后将其巧妙对应到试管上。当我们急于修补问题时，关键在于不纠结于内容本身，而是关注听众对内容产生的情感共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. So the advice here essentially is you're trying to find a story to tell about something, to help you convince someone of something. You want to think about what is the theme of this problem that I have? What is the meaning behind it and what is the message?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。所以这里的建议本质上是，你要试着找到一个故事来讲述某件事，从而帮助你说服别人相信某个观点。你需要思考我遇到的这个问题的主题是什么？它背后的意义是什么？传达的信息又是什么？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah. Usually one of those. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过通常都是这样的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you also touched back on make something in the story relate to something personal about you so that people are like, oh, I'm a runner too. I got to pay attention to this guy. Or I'm shopping. I shop all the time for apples.
turns.zh: 然后你还提到要让故事中的某些内容与你个人的经历相关，这样人们就会想，哦，我也是个跑步爱好者。我得关注这个人。或者我经常买苹果。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yes. See, so we're stacking strategies, which is a really good thing to do. So we're pulling in all of the things I've talked about and it really makes for a powerful moment for people and a memorable moment. Because the most important thing is that we're becoming memorable. We are in a conference amongst other scientists and we're actually the one who's being remembered.
turns.zh: 对。看，所以我们是在整合各种策略，这确实是个很棒的做法。我们把我提到的所有方法都整合起来，就能为听众创造一个震撼人心的时刻，一个难忘的瞬间。因为最重要的是，我们要让人记住。我们身处一个科学家云集的会议中，最终成为被记住的那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So that was the band-aid approach. Then there's the way you recommend it was just build a bank of stories. I imagine this is where the Homework for Life framework you recommend comes from. So maybe let's transition talk about that. Because I think that has a lot of benefits beyond even just coming up with a bunch of story ideas.
turns.zh: 所以这就是权宜之计。然后你推荐的另一种方法就是积累故事库。我猜你提到的"终身作业"框架就是源自这里吧。那我们可以接着聊聊这个框架。我觉得它的好处远不止是能想出很多故事创意。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah. It's the most important thing that I teach. Whether or not you're ever going to speak in your life. If you plan on being a hermit and going off into the woods and never speaking to someone again, you should be doing Homework for Life regardless. It's a process I came up with maybe 15 years ago now. Essentially when I began telling stories on stages, I fell in love with it immediately, and I got worried that I was going to run out of stories. I saw a lot of storytellers on stages performing, and they would tell the same 6, 7, 8 stories every time, and I didn't want to be that guy. I wanted to have a brand new story every time I took the stage. (01:07:25): So in a fit of panic, I decided to assign myself homework being an elementary school teacher, it's natural for me to have that inclination. So I just decided every day before I go to bed, I'm going to look back on the day and find one moment that would've been worth telling as a story. Even if it wasn't really worth telling, I was going to write it down. Now I don't write the whole thing down. That's crazy. It's not doable. What I do is I took an Excel spreadsheet, two columns, the date, and then I stretched the B column across. And in that B column, essentially the length of the computer screen, that's where I write my story. (01:07:59): My goal was I find one new moment per month. 12 new stories per year. That would be amazing. Instead, something far more amazing happens. I discovered that my life is filled with more stories than I will ever have time to tell. And I'm not a unicorn. Thousands of people all over the world are doing the same thing right now and discovering that their lives are filled with stories. Moments like Eileen, which 20 years ago, I would've forgotten that moment within days, and now I've held onto it because it's going to be a Homework for Life moment. (01:08:29): So I start writing those moments down, and I discovered that I'm developing a lens for storytelling. I see the moments that I did not see before. In fact, I just did some analysis for my new book. In the first year I did Homework for Life I found 1.8 moments per day. So you can find more than one. Eventually I started recording more than one. So 1.8 moments per day. I now find 7.6 moments per day. It's not because my life is more interesting. It's because I have a better lens and I understand what to look for, what to see, and what is worth remembering. So I've become a person who has an endless number of stories like Boris. (01:09:07): Boris does Homework for Life. It's why whenever we meet, he's got three new stories to tell me. And then we work on the stories and then figure out the business applications for them. So it's so important because what we do is we throw our lives away. People say that time flies and it doesn't. What happens is it goes by unaccounted. If you can only remember 89 days of 365 in a year, of course time flies. Because you had 365 and you only remember 89. It's going to feel like it went by quickly. It's not going by quickly, you're just failing to account for each day. And each day has something worth remembering. Homework for Life is the acknowledgement that every single day should have something. (01:09:48): The prompt that I actually use for myself is this. I say, if someone kidnapped my family and said, "You can't have them back until you stand on a stage and tell a story about something that happened today, what would you tell?" That was what I would think in my head every night, and then I would write it down. To be honest, nowadays, I'm not sitting down at the end of the day and writing them all down. I'm recording them as the day goes on. My laptop is around me, my phone is around me. When I hear something. My son says a bit of dialogue I can't believe he just said. I see something for the first time or the last time, or a stray thought enters my mind. I have a new thought that I had not occurred before, all of those become moments for Homework for Life. (01:10:28): Not everyone becomes a story. I did some analysis on this too. About 10% of the things that I write down ultimately either become a story or a part of a story, but the other 90% it's just as valuable. Because I'm holding onto my days. And the other amazing thing that happens is once you start doing this, you'll crack open. And all of the stories that you've left from the past, the ones you've forgotten, they'll start to rise up. They'll bubble up. And I include those in my Homework for Life too as memories. Because once you start looking through the lens of storytelling, you see something like you see Eileen find confidence, and suddenly your brain connects to other students or moments in your life or moments in your children's life, where confidence was an issue and you think, oh, that's right. It's just like that kid. (01:11:11): And now I have another moment that I've recovered from the past. A day has returned to me. It enters my Homework for Life, and suddenly I have more stories than I ever have time to tell. And it's not just me. Like I said, thousands of people all over the world, my own children and my students do Homework for Life. And all of them will tell you it's the most valuable thing that you can do.
turns.zh:
是啊。这是我教导的最重要的一件事。无论你未来是否会开口说话。即便你打算做个隐士，躲进深山再也不与人交谈，你也应该坚持“终身作业”。这个方法是我大约15年前想出来的。当我开始在舞台上讲故事时，立刻就爱上了这份职业，但当时我担心自己会故事枯竭。看着很多讲故事的人每次表演时都讲着六、七、八个老掉牙的故事，我可不想成为那样的人。我希望每次上台都能有全新的故事。（01:07:25）：于是我临时抱佛脚，效仿小学老师的作业习惯——毕竟我天生就喜欢规划日程。每天睡前，我都会回顾当天，寻找一个值得讲述的故事。即便这个故事不值得分享，我也会把它记下来。现在我不会完整记录所有细节，那太耗费精力了。我用Excel表格，两列：日期，然后把B列拉宽至屏幕长度。每天的精彩瞬间就写在那里。（01:07:59）：我的目标是每月发现一个新故事，每年12个。这已经很了不起了。但更令人惊喜的是，生活中的故事远超想象。我并非天赋异禀。全球数千人正在践行“终身作业”，发现自己的生活充满故事。像20年前艾琳的故事，若非坚持记录，我早已遗忘。而现在这个瞬间成为我人生宝库中的一笔财富。（01:08:29）：我开始记录这些瞬间，逐渐培养出讲故事的敏锐力。以前忽视的瞬间如今清晰可见。事实上，我刚为新书做过分析。第一年执行“终身作业”时，我每天发现1.8个精彩瞬间。后来增加到多个。如今每天7.6个。这并非生活更精彩，而是我掌握了观察技巧，知道该留意什么、记住什么。如今我像鲍里斯一样，故事源源不断。（01:09:07）：鲍里斯坚持“终身作业”。每次见面，他总有三个新故事要分享。我们一起打磨故事，挖掘商业应用。这至关重要，因为我们在浪费生命。人们说时间飞逝，但其实时间被忽视了。如果你一年365天只记得89天，那时间当然过得快。问题不在于时间飞逝，而在于你未能记录每一天。每一天都值得铭记。“终身作业”就是确认每一天都应有所收获。（01:09:48）：我给自己设定的思考题是：如果有人绑架我的家人，说除非你站在舞台上讲今天发生的故事，否则不放人，否则你会讲什么？这就是我每晚在脑海中构思的故事。如今，我不再为此冥思苦想了。
这一天结束后，我会把所有这些片段都记录下来。我会随时把它们记在笔记本里，笔记本就在我身边，手机也在我身边。当我听到某些话语时，比如儿子说出的一些让我难以置信的对白；当我第一次或最后一次看到某个景象时，或者某个突如其来的念头在我脑海中闪现；当我突然产生一个前所未有的想法时，所有这些都成为《生活作业》系列的素材。（01:10:28）并非每件事都能成为一个故事。我对此也做过分析。大约10%我记录下来的内容最终会成为一个故事或故事的一部分，但其他90%的素材同样珍贵。因为我正在记录自己的每一天。而更神奇的是，一旦你开始这样做，你会突然打开记忆的闸门。那些被你遗忘的往事会重新浮出水面。我也会把这些记忆收录进《生活作业》中，因为一旦你用讲故事的视角去审视生活，你会发现某些片段。比如看到艾琳找回自信的那一刻，你的脑海中会联想到自己或他人生命中曾面临自信挑战的时刻，或者孩子成长过程中类似的经历。这时你会恍然大悟，原来这段经历如此相似。（01:11:11）现在，我又从往事中挖掘出一个新的片段。一段逝去的日子重新回到我的记忆中，被收录进《生活作业》里。我突然发现，自己要讲述的故事比能讲的时间还要多。而这不仅仅发生在我身上。我说过，世界各地有成千上万的人都在践行《生活作业》，包括我的孩子和学生。他们都会告诉你，这是你能做的最有价值的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think you touched on this. It's not just to collect a bunch of stories. There's a therapeutic element to this too, that you talk about.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得你已经提到这一点了。这不只是收集一堆故事。这里面还有一种治疗的元素，正如你所讲的。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah. Absolutely. Many therapeutic elements. First is you're recovering your time and slowing time down, which is beautiful. My kids are 14 and 11. Thank goodness I started Homework for Life just about when Clara was first born. Because they feel 14 and 11 to me. They don't feel like they were just born yesterday, which for a lot of parents, they do. Lots of parents say things like, "Oh, my God, you're not going to believe what my kids said. I got to write it down." But nobody writes it down. You're not going to believe what my kid said is in Homework for Life for me. So I'm holding onto the moments, stretching out time. You also start to do things like you start to see patterns in your life that you don't realize, unless you really think about your life. And I think you should. Storytellers tend to be slightly self-centered in a positive way, meaning we afford ourselves time to think about ourselves. (01:12:22): You start to see patterns if you start doing this. So I think what I talk about in my book is I always tell people, my wife and I never fight. We've never raised our voices to each other. We really don't ever argue. But I noticed in my Homework for Life a moment when she had asked me to put in the air conditioners before I had central air in the house, and I hated it. I hated it because we agreed to never buy a house without central air. And every year the air conditioners somehow get heavier. I don't understand the physics behind it, but every year it's worse. (01:12:50): And she always asks on the 98 degree day, "Hey, can you put the air conditioners in?" And there was a day when I was like, "No, I'm not going to do it. It's really hot." And she was like, "Okay, no problem." And then 10 minutes later, I'm in the basement pulling them out, complaining, grumbling, arguing. Only to myself banging them on purpose so she can hear. She's like, "What's going on?" I'm like, "I'm putting in the air conditioners." So that becomes a Homework for Life moment. (01:13:13): And then a month later, she asks me to mow the lawn, on a 98 degree day. And I said, "I'm not going to mow the lawn. I'm busy and it's really hot." And she goes, "Okay, no problem. Maybe tomorrow." And then I sit for a while and I stew. And then I'm mowing the lawn, but I'm doing it aggressively. I'm running and just angrily mowing the lawn. And when I see these patterns, I suddenly go, "Oh, I do fight with my wife, on my own." I fight in a way that she's not aware I'm doing it. I yell at her through chores and she's not aware that it's even happening. That becomes a story that couples love. They think it's hilarious. (01:13:48): You also start to see stories that you would've never seen. So it was a day last May when the neighbors to my left and the neighbors to my right came over to the house and had a cookout, the first one of the year. And that was a day when I didn't find anything in the day. I had one moment, which is very unusual for me. And I remember thinking, "Really, all you got is you had a cookout with the neighbors, that's the best you got?" It's not even really a story. But it was the best I had so I wrote it down and I moved on. About four months later, the neighbors to our left announced they were getting divorced. It devastated us. Because they have two kids. We've got this big communal backyard with the three houses. Three boys to the right, two kids to the left, friends. Couldn't believe it that they're getting divorced. Known each other since high school. We just never saw it coming. (01:14:33): One day later, neighbors to the right announced they're getting divorced. Left and right within a day of each other. And it becomes a story about how you never understand what's going on in a marriage unless you're in that house. But I don't have that moment in May when there were three couples on a porch, one of them was happy. I thought all three were happy. I don't get that moment unless I'm doing Homework for Life, and I write it down, and now I see a trajectory of a story. I have the opposite. Now I actually have an opposite moment which is I'm serving hot dogs to people I think are happy, but they're only pretending to be happy for our sake. And then they're returning to their homes, to discord and eventually to disillusion of a marriage. So Homework for Life gives you all of that that you don't normally have in life because we tend to live day by day, and we leave that last day behind.
turns.zh:
是的。绝对有。里面有很多治疗性的元素。首先，你在找回自己的时间、放慢时间的流逝，这很美妙。我的两个孩子，一个14岁，一个11岁。谢天谢地，我在克拉拉刚出生时就开始写《家庭作业》了。因为对他们来说，我觉得他们分别14岁和11岁。他们不会让我觉得他们昨天才出生，而很多父母都会有这种感觉。很多父母会说：“天哪，你绝对不会相信我的孩子说了什么。我得把它写下来。”但没人真的去写。我在《家庭作业》里记录下这些瞬间，延缓了时间的流逝。

你还会开始做一些事情，比如发现生活中的模式，除非你真的去思考自己的生活，否则你不会注意到这些模式。我觉得我书里讲的这些东西很重要。我和妻子从不吵架，从不提高嗓门，也从不争执。但我在《家庭作业》里发现了一个瞬间。她让我在家里装中央空调之前先装空调，我讨厌这件事，因为我们约定过买房绝不装中央空调。每年空调越来越重。我不明白其中的物理原理，但情况越来越糟。

（01:12:22）有一天她在98度高温的天气里问：“嘿，能把空调装起来吗？”那天我说：“不，我不装。太热了。”她说：“好的，没关系。”10分钟后，我在地下室把空调拿出来，抱怨不休，发脾气。但其实我是在故意撞东西让她听到。她问：“怎么了？” 我说：“我在装空调。” 这成了《家庭作业》里的一个瞬间。

（01:13:13）一个月后，她在98度高温的天气里让我修剪草坪。我说：“我不修剪草坪。我很忙，而且太热了。” 她说：“好的，没关系。明天再说吧。” 然后我坐了一会儿，越想越生气，最后还是去修剪了。但我修剪得很凶，跑来跑去，大发雷霆。当我意识到这些模式时，我突然说：“哦，我确实在和妻子吵架，虽然她自己没意识到。” 我通过家务事向她发脾气，而她根本没察觉。这成了夫妻们爱听的故事，他们觉得特别搞笑。

（01:13:48）你还会开始看到以前从未注意到的事情。比如去年五月的一天，我左边和右边的邻居来我家烧烤，那是他们今年第一次烧烤。那天我一整天都没发现什么特别的事，只有一个瞬间对我来说很不寻常。我记得当时想：“真的吗？你就发现和邻居烧烤了？这就是你今天最大的收获？” 这甚至算不上一个故事。但这是我当天最好的收获，所以我把它写下来，然后继续生活。大约四个月后，左边的邻居宣布他们要离婚了。这让我们很震惊。因为他们有两个孩子。我们三户人家共用一个大后院，右边三个男孩，左边两个孩子，都是朋友。真不敢相信他们要离婚了。他们从高中就认识了。我们完全没预料到。

（01:14:33）一天后，右边的邻居也宣布了离婚消息。
他们要离婚了。两对夫妻几乎在同一天先后宣布分道扬镳。这成了一个警示：除非你亲身置身于那段婚姻关系中，否则永远无法理解其中奥秘。但五月那天我站在门廊上，见证了三对夫妻的场景，其中一对洋溢着幸福。我曾以为三对都是如此美满。若非参与《生活作业》节目，记录下那些瞬间，我或许永远无法洞察其背后的真相。如今我经历了相反的情景——为那些看似幸福的家庭供应热狗，可他们不过是为我们虚伪装欢。最终他们还是要回到家中，面对婚姻的裂痕与幻灭。《生活作业》为你呈现了这些生活中的缺失片段——因为我们总是忙于应付日常，往往将最重要的日子留在身后。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got tingles listening to that story. For someone that's now motivated to try this. I know there's a template that we'll link to in the show notes where you give people, it's very simple, but I think seeing it will be helpful. But what's something someone could do tonight to start on this process and maybe set a habit to do? How do you actually go about doing this?
turns.zh: 听完那个故事，我浑身起鸡皮疙瘩。对于现在正准备尝试的人来说，我知道我们会在节目笔记中附上一个模板，内容非常简单，但我觉得看一看会很有帮助。但今晚人们能做些什么来开始这个过程，或许还能养成一个习惯呢？具体该怎么做呢？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Well, they have to start Homework for Life. And I have a TED talk about it that I go on for 17 minutes about. So I suggest watching it because you'll just get more than what I just told you and I think that's important. And you have to decide to do it every single day, even on the day when the best you have is a cookout. If that's all you got, that's what you got, and you write it down. You have to have some faith too, that it's going to happen over time. Remember, I started with 1.8 and now I'm up to 7.6. And that's over more than 12 years it takes for me to make that jump. (01:16:12): So in the beginning, you're not going to be very good at it. You're not going to see the right things, and that's just the way it is. If I go back to my original Homework for Life, I see myself looking for stories. And you're not really looking for stories. You're just looking for moments that touch your heart, touch your mind. That's all you're really hoping for. And some of those will become stories. So you've got to start Homework for Life right away. And then if you can just find some people who are willing to listen and begin telling some stories, that's really helpful because most people are unwilling to listen. There's not a lot of good listeners in the world. Everyone says they're a great listener, but active listening is a skill that most people do not possess in any way whatsoever. But if you find people who are willing to listen, you got to start telling stories. You got to start practicing in meaningful ways. And your first stories aren't going to be great. But the good news is most people's stories are terrible. Most storytelling in the world is not very good. So if you put a little thought into what you're about to say, you're going to be better. Because storytelling is not about facility with the language or your vocabulary. It's all about decision-making. That's all it is. (01:17:14): Storytellers are people who think before they speak. They make strategical tactical decisions before they speak. And ultimately, they make enough good decisions to entertain people. Ultimately, no matter what you're doing, whether I am teaching a fifth grader how to behave better, or presenting a new product for a large company, or helping someone deliver an all hands, the first and most important thing you have to be is entertaining. You have to entertain or people will not listen to you. So you got to practice, you got to get reps.
turns.zh: 嗯，他们得先开始“终身作业”。我还做过一个关于它的TED演讲，讲了17分钟。所以我建议大家去看看，因为你会得到比我刚刚告诉你的更多信息，我觉得这很重要。你必须决定每天都坚持做这件事，即便当天你最多只能做个户外烧烤。如果只能做到这点，那就做这点，然后把它写下来。你还得有信心，相信随着时间推移，事情会慢慢改变。记住，我从1.8分开始，现在已经达到7.6分了。这花了我超过12年的时间才取得这样的进步。（01:16:12）所以一开始，你做得不会很好。你看不到正确的东西，这很正常。如果回看我最初的“终身作业”视频，我发现自己当时在寻找故事。而你当时其实不是在寻找故事，你只是在寻找能触动你心灵、启发你思考的瞬间。这才是你真正期待的。其中一些会成为故事。所以你得马上开始“终身作业”。然后，如果你能找到愿意倾听的人并开始讲述故事，那就太有帮助了，因为大多数人都不愿意倾听。世界上没有很多善于倾听的人。他们都说自己很善于倾听，但主动倾听是一项大多数人完全不具备的技能。但如果你能找到愿意倾听的人，就得开始讲故事了。你得开始有意义地练习。你的第一个故事不会很棒，但好消息是大多数人的故事都很糟糕。世界上大多数讲故事的人都不太擅长。所以如果你能在即将要说的内容上多花点心思，你就会做得更好。因为讲故事不是关于语言流畅度或词汇量的。关键在于决策力。仅此而已。（01:17:14）讲故事的人会在说话前先思考。他们在说话前会做出策略性的决定。最终，他们会做出足够多的好决定来娱乐听众。无论你在做什么，无论是教五年级学生如何更好地表现，还是为大公司展示新产品，或是帮助某人召开全员会议，最重要的一件事就是要娱乐人。你必须娱乐人，否则人们就不会听你说话。所以你得练习，得多多实践。

turns.en: I want to talk about public speaking skills, but just to close the loop on that. So if someone was trying to do this Homework for Life exercises, the idea, would you recommend at night before they go to sleep, open up Google Sheets on their phone and just add something? Is there something else you'd recommend?
turns.zh: 我想谈谈公开演讲技巧，但先把这个话题收尾。所以如果有人想尝试这些“终身作业”练习，你会建议他们晚上睡前在手机上打开Google Sheets，添加一些内容吗？你还有什么其他建议吗？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: No. Yeah. That's what I would do. Although ideally, as you go through...
turns.zh: 不。是的。我会这么做。不过理想情况下，随着你不断练习……

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: No. Yeah, that's what I would do. Although ideally, as you go through the day, things get forgotten quickly. Your son says something hilarious and by the end of the night you can't remember what it was. So if you can start sort of tracking it through the day a little bit, maybe you make it a habit where at lunchtime you're going to ask yourself what happened that morning? And when you get home from work, you're going to say what happened in the afternoon? And then in the evening you're going to say what happened since then? And then sort of take a whole view of the day and then be open to those memories, allow them to come back. I record them in my Homework for Life as memory, sort of a capital M-E-M-O-R-Y. Because what happens is you start to build up so many homework for life memories that you get confused. (01:18:39): You're like, what? When did I see a deer? And then I go, oh, that's a story from when I was 14. But you get confused because it's sitting on when you're 38 years old. So you mark them as memories. You hold onto them, you put them into spreadsheets because eventually you're going to want to move that data around and keep track of it in some meaningful way. But yeah, get started today because if you don't, you will lose today. Every day that you don't do homework for life is a day that is going to be lost to you forever.
turns.zh: 别这样。是啊，我也会这么做。不过理想情况下，随着一天的推移，事情会很快被遗忘。比如你儿子说了什么搞笑的话，但到了晚上你却记不起来了。所以如果你能在一天中稍微记录一下，也许可以养成一个习惯，比如午餐时问自己今天早上发生了什么，下了班后再回想一下下午发生了什么，晚上再回顾一下之后的事情。然后全面回顾一天的经历，敞开心扉接纳那些记忆。我把这些记录在《生活作业》里用大写的"M-E-M-O-R-Y"标注。因为你会积累太多生活作业式的记忆，以至于感到困惑。（01:18:39）你会说，什么？我什么时候见过鹿啊？然后我说，哦，那是我14岁时的故事。但你会感到困惑，因为这段记忆发生在你38岁的时候。所以你把它们标记为记忆，保存下来，放进电子表格里，因为你最终会想以某种有意义的方式整理这些数据。但没错，从今天开始行动吧，如果不行动，你就会失去今天。每一天不做生活作业就是永久失去的一天。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just very practically, you recommend like Google Sheets, I imagine is what you use?
turns.zh: 说到实际操作，你推荐用Google Sheets，我猜你用的是这个吧？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: I actually use old-fashioned Excel, but yes, Google Sheets would work too, because I started so long ago, right, Excel was the thing I used, and Excel is the thing I still use. I mean, it's backed up in 19 places because it's the most precious thing I have other than my wife and children, cats. But yeah, that's what I would suggest to use.
turns.zh: 我其实用的是老式的Excel，但Google Sheets也可以，因为我用了太久了。对，我从很久以前就开始用Excel了，现在还在用。这意味着它被备份了19份，因为除了妻子和孩子、猫之外，它是我最珍视的东西了。但没错，这就是我建议使用的。

turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Just a couple more questions before our very exciting lightning round. In your book, you say that you've only been nervous twice on stage giving a story. Most people, I don't know, is that [inaudible 01:19:36].
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，在我们激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，还有几个问题。你在书中提到，你在台上讲故事时只紧张过两次。大多数人，我不知道，是不是[01:19:36听不清]。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah, that's true. I'm like,-
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。我就觉得——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: I can remember the two times. It was yeah, it was PTSD related and Seth Meyers cost of ticket related.
turns.zh: 我记得那两次。一次是创伤后应激障碍相关的，一次是关于Seth Meyers演出票价的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I remember that story.
turns.zh: 哦，我记得那个故事。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So most people are not like you. Most people are nervous, including me, every single time I get on stage, tell a story. What advice do you give people to help them get better with the nerves of getting on stage and telling a story? Classically, it's the thing people fear most in life.
turns.zh: 好的。所以大多数人都不像你。他们都很紧张，包括我，每次上台讲故事都很紧张。你能给人们什么建议，帮助他们克服上台讲故事时的紧张情绪吗？传统上来说，这是人们一生中最害怕的事情。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Well, the first thing you have to understand is that 98% of your nervousness is actually before you begin speaking. Once you begin speaking, almost all of your nervousness falls away, and that is the experience of most people. So what you're really suffering is from pre-talk nervousness. And when you find that out, that's kind of a relief because if you do it enough. Someone just spoke in the Netherlands, and today I'm waiting to find out how it went. He spoke it for the Florida State Legislature, same topic, and he was really nervous about going into today. He was also really nervous speaking to a bunch of scientists in the Netherlands. But I told him, I said, "After you began speaking in the Netherlands, once the talk began, how nervous were you?" And he said, "Oh, actually, when I began speaking, I was pretty okay. I was incredibly nervous before the talk." And I said, "Well, that makes sense." (01:20:49): So if you own the fact or you believe the fact that, oh, most of my nervousness comes before the talk, but once I start speaking, I'm pretty good. That's really relieving for a lot of people because what we imagine is that we're nervous while we're talking, which is often not the case, particularly if you're kind of prepared, if you know what you're talking about. So be aware that most of your nervousness happens before you speak, and that's a normal thing, and you're just going to have to accept that until some day when perhaps it starts to go away through repetition, through continued performance on a stage. For some people, they're always nervous. I was performing with, I won't say her name, but someone who you have watched on television before, and we were both backstage and I was chatting up the room and she finally said to me, this very famous person, "Would you stop talking? Because the rest of us are trying to keep information in our head and stay calm." I'm a terrible person backstage because I'm always calm, I never care. (01:21:45): So I have to sort of sequester myself from these people because I torture them. But once she began speaking, all of her nerves fell away. So that's a good thing to know. The other thing to know that's really great is everyone's nervous, except for me. I'm the only monster in the world. So if you're feeling nervous, you're just like everyone else, including a very famous person who you see on TV all the time. That person was nervous, you're nervous, you're in the same camp, right, you're in the same boat. And then preparation is going to reduce your level of nervousness. One of the things that I tell people to do that is most helpful is it's good to practice your talk or practice your pitch, whatever you're doing, but one of the best ways to prepare for it is to record it and listen to it. (01:22:26): Listen to it passively, listen to it while your grocery shopping, listen to it while you're folding laundry, doing the dishes. What happens is, I really believe this, as you start to listen to it over and over again, it just sort of seeps into your soul, and so it becomes part of you. I have done this technique. I've told a story a decade ago, haven't told it since. Someone hears it on YouTube and says, "Hey, can you tell that story at our event?" I say, "Yes". I can listen to it once and it comes right out again because I allowed it to sort of sink into my memory in the same way that When Harry Met Sally has sunk into your wife's memory. She can replay that movie in her mind probably perfectly. If you listen to your talk enough, you will get to the point where you can retell it with ease. (01:23:09): The other thing you can do is some active listening with it. Most people don't forget their talk. They forget the transitions in their talk. So I'm talking about this, but then I got to transition to this, then I got to transition to this. So when I'm listening to my stories or a talk that I'm going to give, I'm playing a game with myself. (01:23:26): So I'm listening and I go, oh, okay, this is closing out and the next thing I have to talk about is this, and then the next thing I have to talk about is this. And if I don't know what I'm going to, if I'm like, Ooh, what am I going to next? That's where I go, oh, I got to create a mnemonic there. I got to create a bit of memorization there to train myself for that transition. Once you're in a new section of a talk, even if you're following it up a little, you're going to be okay because you're like, oh, I got to talk about the data related to the this or the that. And if it doesn't come out perfectly, you still know what you're talking about. (01:23:55): But what happens when you're done with the data related to this or that, you go, ah damn, what am I supposed to do next? Right. So we're working on building those transitions. Before a talk or before a story let's say I will do something like I'm going to start in the car and then I'm going to get out into the store, and then I'm going to head out to the parking lot, and then I'm going to be in the park, and then it's three weeks later. I don't tell myself the story. I'm just bouncing between the scenes because once I know the scenes and I know, okay, there's seven scenes, and here they are, and here's the transitions. Again, if I follow up each scene, that's okay because I'm going to get the information out. It might not come out as perfectly as I hoped. You also, if you can avoid memorizing, that'll save you a ton of suffering because memorizers, they're the most tortured souls in the world. So avoid that if all possible. Remember your talk without memorizing your talk.
turns.zh:
嗯，首先你要明白的是，你98%的紧张感实际上是在演讲开始前产生的。一旦开始演讲，几乎所有的紧张感都会消失，这是大多数人的经历。所以你真正需要应对的是演讲前的紧张感。当你意识到这一点时，会感到如释重负，因为只要你足够练习。最近有人在荷兰演讲，我现在正等着听反馈。他在佛罗里达州议会做演讲，讲同一个主题，但去荷兰演讲前特别紧张。还有人在荷兰面对一群科学家发言时也很紧张。但我问他："演讲开始后，你有多紧张？"他说："其实刚开始时还挺镇定的，真正紧张的是演讲前。" 我说："这就对了。"（01:20:49）所以如果你能接受这个事实——即紧张感主要在演讲前产生，而演讲后就会缓解——这对很多人来说是个巨大的解脱。我们总以为自己在演讲时紧张，但事实并非如此，尤其是如果你准备充分、对演讲内容了如指掌的话。要知道，紧张感大多在演讲前产生，这是正常现象，你必须接受这一点，直到通过不断练习、多次登台表演后逐渐消失。有些人永远紧张。我曾和一位不便透露姓名的人合作过（相信你们在电视上见过她），我们在后台聊天时，她终于对我说："你能别说话吗？我们得集中精力记台词，保持冷静。" 我在后台就是个话痨，从不紧张。（01:21:45）所以我不得不远离这些人，因为我太折磨他们了。但她一开始演讲，紧张感就消失了。这点很重要。还有个很棒的发现：除了我，每个人都会紧张。我是这个世界上唯一的怪物。所以如果你感到紧张，和其他人一样，包括你在电视上常见的名人。他们紧张，你也紧张，你们都在同一条船上。这时候准备工作就能减轻紧张感。最有效的准备方法之一是练习演讲或推销词，无论你做什么，但最有效的准备方式之一是录制下来反复听。（01:22:26）被动听取，比如在买菜时听，叠衣服时听，洗碗时听。我深信，只要反复听，它会渗透到你的灵魂深处，成为你的一部分。我用过这个方法。十年前讲过一个故事，此后再没讲过。有人在YouTube上听到后，说："能在我们的活动上讲那个故事吗？"我说："没问题。" 我只需听一遍就能脱口而出，就好像《当哈利遇到莎莉》深深印在你妻子脑海里一样。她能完美重现那部电影的情节。只要你反复听演讲，最终就能轻松复述。
（01:23:09）：你还可以做的是进行主动倾听。大多数人不会忘记自己讲的内容，而是会忘记讲话中的过渡环节。所以我现在讲这个，但接下来我得过渡到那个，再过渡到另一个。当我听自己的故事或准备要做的演讲时，我会和自己玩一个游戏。（01:23:26）：所以我边听边想，哦，好，现在要结束了，接下来要讲的是这个，然后是那个。如果我不知道接下来该讲什么，就会想，哦，接下来该讲什么了？这时候我就想，哦，我得在这儿创造一个记忆点。得在这儿编个小口诀，训练自己完成过渡。一旦进入演讲的新段落，即便你只是稍作补充，也没关系，因为你会想，哦，我得讲讲和这个或那个相关的数据。即使讲得不完美，你也知道自己在讲什么。（01:23:55）：但当讲完和这个或那个相关的数据后，你会说，啊，糟糕，接下来该讲什么了？对。所以我们要努力打造这些过渡环节。比如在演讲或讲故事前，我会这样安排：先从车里开始讲，然后到商店，再到停车场，最后到公园，再三周后。不用把整个故事都讲出来，我只是在场景之间切换。因为一旦你熟悉了这些场景，知道有七个场景，知道过渡在哪儿，那么每个场景都按顺序讲就没问题了。即使讲得不完美，也没关系。还有，如果能避免死记硬背，会省去很多痛苦，因为那些背书的人真是世界上最折磨自己的人。所以尽可能避免背书。不用背书也能记住你的演讲内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me, a friend of mine gave a TED Talk and he shared that they give you this advice that people are different kind of learners. Some are audio learners, some are visual. So if you're like an audio learner, listening to it is the most helpful. Some it's seeing the script.
turns.zh: 这让我想起，我的一个朋友在TED演讲中提到，他们会给出这样一个建议：不同的人有不同的学习方式。有些人是听觉型学习者，有些人是视觉型学习者。所以如果你属于听觉型学习者，那么听讲解是最有效的。而有些人则需要看文字教材。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And looking at it,-
turns.zh: 而看文字教材——

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: And I'm very much an auditory learner. The other thing though about listening to it is you just get sick of practicing. It gets so frustrating to practice. So at some point you don't want to say it anymore. So rather than saying it, you start to listen to it. You listen to yourself, tell a story about yourself to yourself, which is the most narcissistic thing you could probably do in the world. But even if you're a visual learner, because it's so annoying to practice eventually, I think listening to it can be really helpful.
turns.zh: 我自己就是典型的听觉型学习者。不过听讲解也有个问题，就是练习得多了会让人感到厌烦。反复练习实在太折磨人了，最后你甚至都不想再说了。所以与其自己说，不如先听听别人的讲解。听自己说话，给自己讲故事，这可能是世界上最自恋的行为了。但即便你是视觉型学习者，面对枯燥的练习最终也会感到厌烦，我觉得听讲解还是很有帮助的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Last question is I want to talk about, I mentioned I bring this up, is the power of saying yes, something that you recommend people say yes to stuff versus no. It reminds me, David Sedaris in a, I don't know, Dave Masterclass video or something, said the same thing. He's just like, "I just say yes to everything because it creates great stories."
turns.zh: 好的。最后一个问题是，我想谈谈我提到的"说yes"的力量，你建议人们多说yes而少说no。这让我想起大卫·塞达里斯在某个视频（比如Dave Masterclass）里说过同样的话。他说：“我对所有事情都说yes，因为这样能创造出精彩的故事。”

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's in his Masterclass talk,-
turns.zh: 是啊，他在Masterclass讲座里提到过——

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: And I just finished Sedaris's Happy-Go-Lucky, which is a great book. I love him.
turns.zh: 我刚读完塞达里斯的《快乐无忧》，这本书太棒了。我超爱他。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So I'd love to hear your advice here for people just to give them a little bit of a final takeaway.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。所以我很想听听你对大家的建议，让他们能收获最后的启发。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Sure. So I'm going to disagree with Sedaris a little bit. Nah, I won't disagree with him by saying, yes, you do end up with some great stories, but that's not the purpose of the yes. There's actually a book, a storytelling book in the world that I'm not going to mention, and it talks about how to find great stories and it says, go do crazy things and you'll have great stories. I disagree. Fundamentally first, that's a foolish way to live your life. And also some of the best stories I tell, I think the best stories I tell are about tiny moments in our lives where nothing extraordinary happens except everything in our head, right? Most stories that I tell, if you had actually witness the moment of transformation or realization, you would've never known it was happening because most things that happen to us happen in our heads. (01:26:34): It's not while we're hanging from a cliff, right, for our dear life that we suddenly have a revelation. It's usually like we're walking across a parking lot and suddenly something hits us that's been building up for three weeks, but now it's hit us walking across the parking lot. So the reason we say yes to everything is if you don't say yes, what you're essentially saying is, I am so presumptuous that I understand what's on the other side of that door already even though I've never set foot beyond that door. Right. I just know so much about the world that I know that what's behind that door is not for me. And I think that's foolish and arrogant and full of hubris that is not helping anyone in any way. (01:27:19): So I say when someone offers you an opportunity, as crazy as it is, as ridiculous, as much as you don't want to do it, which many times in my life, the yeses that I have said about something I did not want to do, but forced myself to do it because of my belief system have resulted in the best and most extraordinary opportunities of my life. A yes can always become a no, right? Yes, I will try that. I step through the door, I give it a try, I spend some time with it. I look around and I say, you know what? Not for me. I step back through and I close the door. (01:27:54): But so often in life, people don't step through the door. They're too afraid. They've already prejudged the opportunity in some way. They fail to see the benefits of it or the value because they can't see that because they haven't gone through the door. And then there's this ridiculous belief in the world that we're supposed to learn to say no so that we can sort of sequester our time and make it as meaningful as possible, which sounds really terrible to me. The problem is you're going to be 100 someday, and when you're 100, no one is going to be asking you to step through any more doors, and at that point, you're going to look into the past and you're going to say, there were a lot of doors I didn't step through, right, and you're not going to be thinking, I'm so glad I didn't because I allowed myself to stay on the one path that I knew was going to be good for me. (01:28:46): I just think that there is no one good path that's good for you. I think there's a multitude of paths, and they're all great, and a few of them are terrible, but you find out which ones are terrible by stepping through the door, deciding this is not for me and coming back. So I think most of the time people say no because they're afraid. And when someone asks me to do something that scares me, that is when I run to that thing as quickly as possible with all of my might as terrified as I am, because I know that it's the things that frighten me are often the things that are the best for me. (01:29:19): So we say yes with the acknowledgement that we can say no eventually, but a yes can lead to extraordinary things. And if you watch my TED Talk on saying yes, you'll see that yeses just lead to these extraordinary chains where you said yes to something you didn't want to say yes to, and suddenly it forced you to meet someone who you never would've met, who opened a different door for you. And I mean, the causal chain that you can sort of create by saying an odd yes is extraordinary.
turns.zh:
好的。那我要稍微反驳一下塞达里斯的观点了。不，我不会说"是啊，你最终确实能收获一些精彩的故事"来附和他，但这不是问题的关键。世上有一本讲故事的书（我就不点名了），里面教人如何找到好故事，主张去尝试疯狂的事，这样才能收获精彩的故事。我对此不敢苟同。首先，这根本不是明智的生活之道。我觉得自己讲过的最精彩的故事，多源于日常生活中的微小瞬间——没有惊天动地的外在变化，但所有思绪在脑海中翻腾。比如说，你走过停车场时，突然想起积压三周的情绪，此刻情绪爆发。这就是为什么我们要对一切说“是”。因为说“是”意味着：我太自以为是，坚信门后有何物，即便从未踏入那扇门。我自诩对世界了如指掌，以为门后的世界不属于我。这既愚蠢又傲慢，毫无益处。

（01:26:34）所以当有人提供机会时，无论多疯狂、多荒谬、多不愿尝试——我人生中很多次，对不想做的事硬逼自己尝试，结果却收获了最非凡的机遇。一个“是”随时可能变成“否”。比如：“好，我试试看。”跨进门，尝试一番，四处看看后退出：“不适合我。”但现实中太多人不敢跨门。恐惧先入为主，预判机会的价值，错失良机，只因未曾踏入门内。世上还有种荒谬的信念：我们该学会说“不”，才能高效利用时间、提升生活质量。这观点太可怕了。问题是，当你百岁时，再没人请你跨门了。回首往事，你会发现太多未曾尝试的机会。到那时，你不会庆幸自己拒绝了未知，坚守了熟悉的道路。

（01:28:46）我认为没有一条通往成功的标准路径。世间有无数可能性，有些很棒，有些糟糕。只有亲身尝试才能分辨。多数人说“不”是因为恐惧。当有人让我尝试恐惧的事，我会拼命奔向它，因为我知道，正是恐惧让我成长。
对我而言最美好的事物。（01:29:19）：所以我们会说“是”，同时承认自己最终可能选择说“不”，但一个“是”可能会带来非凡的机遇。如果你观看过我关于说“是”的TED演讲，就会发现这些“是”往往会引发一连串意想不到的连锁反应——你可能同意了本不愿答应的事，进而被迫结识了原本无缘相遇的人，而这个人又为你打开了另一扇门。我想说，通过一个看似随意的“是”所能引发的因果链，其产生的效应绝对非同寻常。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There was a quote I often come back to around this, which is, "The cave you fear contains the treasure you seek."
turns.zh: 关于这件事，我常想起一句话：“你所惧怕的洞穴，往往藏着你所追寻的宝藏。”

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah, that's really good. I mean someone, I do standup now quite frequently. I was just in the New York City Comedy Festival, and I do standup because six years ago, one of my buddies sent me an email saying, "Hey, we should do standup." And I replied to him and said, "No, I'm not interested in that." Hit reply. And then I said to myself, "Whoa, why did you just do that?" And I said to myself, "I'm terrified of it." I can tell funny stories and if it's not funny, still telling a story, but if I'm doing standup and I'm not funny, I'm failing. And that's a terrifying thing. (01:30:24): So I immediately sent a second email that said, "Okay, I'm in. When are we doing it?" I have now done standup many, many, many times. That guy who initially asked me to do standup with him has never done it. Not once in his life. He wanted to do it, but he's afraid to step through the door. He's too afraid to do the thing that he challenged me to do that I now do on a regular basis because he challenged me and it's still the thing that probably scares me the most. And therefore, it's the thing that I'm relentlessly trying to do at all times because I know the things that scare me are the things that are the best for me.
turns.zh: 是啊，这话说得真好。比如说，我现在经常表演单口喜剧。前不久我刚参加了纽约喜剧节。六年前，一位好友发邮件邀请我：“嘿，我们一起表演单口喜剧吧。”我回复：“不，我没兴趣。”按下回车键后，又自问：“哇，我为什么要这么说？”接着我意识到：“我太害怕了。” 我能讲有趣的故事，但如果没引起笑声，至少能讲个故事。但如果是单口喜剧，搞笑不了，那就是失败了。这太可怕了。（01:30:24）所以我立刻回了邮件：“好，我加入。什么时候开始？” 从那以后，我表演了无数次单口喜剧。那个最初邀请我一起表演的家伙至今一次都没上台过。他想尝试，却害怕踏出那一步。正因为他挑战了我，而我现在经常表演单口喜剧，所以这事对我来说意义非凡。这也是我不懈追求的目标，因为我知道，令自己害怕的事，往往也是最能造就自己的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Matt, is there anything else you want to share or leave listeners with before we get to your very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。马特，在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: No, I've said enough. They've heard enough from me. Let's go to the lightning round.
turns.zh: 没有了，我已经说得够多了。大家已经听够我的分享了。开始闪电问答吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've covered a lot. Let's do it. Well, welcome to our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 聊了这么多，我们开始吧。欢迎来到激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 你向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Oh, so Nathaniel Philbrick's, Heart of the Sea, which is a non-fiction account of the whale ship Essex, which is the origin of the idea for Moby Dick. The sinking of the Essex is what gave Melville the idea for Moby Dick. It's an extraordinary non-fiction account of the whale ship Essex. So that book for sure. If you have children, but even if you don't, because this is one of those children's books that reads well for adults as Kate DiCamillo's, The Tale of Despereaux. It's a young adult novel. It'll take you two hours to read. I've read it 20 times. It is beautiful and extraordinary and fantastic. And then anything by Jessie Klein, she has two books. The only thing I don't like about her is she only has two books. Actually, Sedaris too, Jessie Klein and David Sedaris. Go read those two people too. I'm actually right now reading Bamford's book, the comedian, what's her first name? Bamford. I have Amy stuck in my head for Amy Sedaris. Maria Bamford's memoir right now I'm reading. Also, extraordinary. So there's four that I am now recommending.
turns.zh: 哦，比如纳撒尼尔·菲尔布里克的《海心》，这是关于捕鲸船埃塞克斯号的非虚构记述，而这艘船正是《白鲸记》的灵感来源。埃塞克斯号的沉没给了梅尔维尔创作《白鲸记》的灵感。这是一本关于埃塞克斯号捕鲸船的非凡非虚构作品。还有凯特·迪卡米洛的《德斯佩罗的故事》。这是一本青少年小说，读起来也很适合成年人。读完只需两个小时。我已经读了20遍。它美丽、非凡、奇妙。还有杰西·克莱恩的作品，她有两本书。我唯一不满的是她只有两本书。说真的，塞达里斯、杰西·克莱恩和大卫·塞达里斯的作品都值得一读。我现在正在读班福德的书，那位喜剧演员，名字叫什么来着？班福德。玛丽亚·班福德的回忆录，我正在读。同样精彩绝伦。所以现在我要推荐这四本书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What's a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Well, for TV shows I enjoyed The Last of Us, which is based on a video game I've never played in my life. Pretty extraordinary as a TV show, both because filled with stakes. Yeah, it's one of those shows they'll kill anyone at any time. And so you're on the edge of your seat. No one is safe, which is fantastic. And then it has this beautiful bottle episode in the middle of the season, which is one of those things where you're in a zombie TV show, which oddly is unlike any zombie TV show I've ever seen. And then there's a beautiful, fantastic episode. There's another one later on that's sort of very similar. It's just great storytelling in a multitude of ways. It's great. And for a movie, the Barbie movie is better than I ever expected it to be, quite frankly, and is proof positive that you can make stories about just about anything, and if they mean something, it's going to do extraordinarily well.
turns.zh:
嗯，电视剧方面我很喜欢《最后生还者》（The Last of Us），这部剧改编自一款我从未玩过的电子游戏。作为电视剧，它相当出色，尤其充满了紧张感——没错，这部剧随时可能让任何角色丧命，让人始终坐立不安。剧中没有人能幸免于难，这点太棒了。而且在本季中段还有一集特别精彩的独立故事，放在僵尸题材电视剧里却独树一帜。还有后续一集也类似，整体来说无论从哪个角度看都是叙事上的杰作，真的很棒。

至于电影方面，坦白说《芭比》比我预期的要好得多，这充分证明只要故事有意义，就能大获成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My next question, I don't know if it makes sense to ask you, it's usually for product people and founders, but the question is, is do you have a favorite interview question you'd like to ask people when you're hiring? Is there anything that comes up when I ask that?
turns.zh: 接下来我想问的问题，可能不太适合问产品人员和创始人，但我想知道，你们在招聘时最喜欢问求职者什么问题？当我问这个问题时，通常会得到哪些答案？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: I guess I'll say it's the question I like to ask people most often maybe when I'm playing golf and things. I don't like to ask people what they do. I like to ask, how did you get into the job you currently have? It's a dangerous question because occasionally I ask people it and they realize they're in their job for weird happenstances that don't relate to what they dreamed of doing. So I've had two people in my life cry while they answered the question because they suddenly understand, I'm doing this because my sister got me into the company 16 years ago. And I go, "Oh, well that's great. Is that what you always wanted to do?" And they say, "No, it's actually still not what I want to do." But I do think that most of the time, how you get a job is more interesting than the actual job you're doing. The answer to that question is more interesting.
turns.zh: 我想说这大概是我最常问别人的问题，尤其是在打高尔夫球之类的时候。我不喜欢问别人做什么工作，而是喜欢问他们如何进入目前的职位。这是个危险的问题，因为有时我问完后，他们才意识到自己进入这份工作是因为一些与梦想毫不相干的巧合。生活中有两个人回答这个问题时流下了眼泪，因为他们突然意识到：“哦，原来是因为16年前我姐姐把我介绍进这家公司啊。”我会说：“哦，挺好的。那这是你一直想做的工作吗？”他们回答：“不，实际上这还不是我真正想做的。” 但我确实认为，大多数情况下，如何获得一份工作比工作本身更有趣。回答这个问题往往更有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like, whether it's an app or something you bought?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品，无论是应用还是你买过的东西？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Well, if you celebrate Christmas for years, I have had an idea on how to design the best Christmas tree stand, and I finally said, someone must've done it. And they did. So I wrote it down for you. It's the Krinner tree stand. The Krinner Tree Genie is extraordinary. It's exactly what I would've designed if I had any ability to design it. It holds up the tree like none other. It takes two seconds. It is everything that the research told me it would do. It's fantastic. If you don't celebrate Christmas, I will tell you that a Power POD, which is a small, it attaches to your keychain and it will charge your phone twice and it just lives on your keychain. So I am never a person who's going, oh no, I don't have any charge left. I have two charges on a Power POD, which lives on my keychain. (01:35:29): You forget it's even there. And then one day you need it and it's fantastic. It's the best one. There's lots of versions of it. The Power POD is the one you want. And then I just bought a hot dog toaster that toasts the hot dogs and the buns at the same time. It's called the Nostalgia Hot Dog Toaster. It looks like it's from the 1950s. It's really beautiful actually. It's the kind of thing you want to put on your counter because it looks fantastic. My son and I love it because we like hot dogs and it'll put two buns and two hot dogs into the toaster. You pull it down, three minutes later you have a hot dog ready to go. You didn't dirty anything. It's not the best hot dog in the world, but hot dogs are pretty great no matter how they're cooked. So I fully support the Nostalgia Hot Dog Toaster.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果你庆祝圣诞节多年的话，我曾想过如何设计最好的圣诞树底座，最后发现肯定有人已经做过了。果然有人做过。所以我把它写下来给你介绍。这就是Krinner树底座。Krinner树精简直太棒了。这正是我如果有设计能力会设计出来的样子。它能稳稳支撑圣诞树，无与伦比。只需两秒钟。它完全符合研究报告中的预期。太棒了。如果你不庆祝圣诞节，我要告诉你，Power POD是个小巧的设备，挂在钥匙链上就能给手机充电两次。（01:35:29）我从不担心手机没电了。Power POD有两次充电量，直接挂在钥匙链上。（01:36:48）你甚至会忘记它的存在。直到某天需要用它时，效果惊人。它堪称最佳之选。虽然有很多类似产品，但Power POD才是你该选的。我刚买了一个热狗烤面包机，能同时烤热狗和面包。叫Nostalgia热狗烤面包机。它看起来像1950年代的款式，设计得特别美。放在台面上很显眼。我和儿子都很喜欢，因为我们爱吃热狗。它能同时烤两个面包和两个热狗。按下按钮，三分钟后热狗就烤好了。一点都不脏。虽然不是世界上最美味的热狗，但无论怎么烤，热狗都很好吃。所以我完全支持Nostalgia热狗烤面包机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are amazing selections. There's also call back to our nostalgia trick for getting to be funny.
turns.zh: 这些选择真是太棒了。这也让我们回想起自己童年时为了搞笑而耍的把戏。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Right. That's true. Yes. Unintended, but I'll take credit for it.
turns.zh: 对啊。这确实改变了我的生活。四年级时，有位老师（我不记得是哪位了，这真让人遗憾），我那天过得很糟糕，表现得和大多数人一样。老师对我说：“听着，积极的心态是成功的关键。”不知为何这句话一直印在我的脑海里。我已经对自己重复了无数次。（01:36:48）如今世上有个人，比我还要积极，我见过的人中，没有比他更积极的。我是个近乎积极得令人讨厌的人，我妻子说我“有时也会情绪低落”。我说：“不会的。因为积极的心态是成功的关键。”这就是我看待生活的方式，总是关注积极面、美好事物。只要有机会，我都会为别人传递这种积极能量。有时这会让人感到烦躁，但我坚信生活的大部分取决于你带入其中的心态。四年级时，“积极的心态是成功的关键”这句话，不知为何在恰当的时机以恰当的方式触动了我，从此便铭记于心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite life motto that you often repeat to yourself, share with friends, either in work or in life?
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这句话甚至不算特别精妙。听起来像是某种幸运签语，

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah, it changed my life really. When I was in fourth grade, a teacher who, and I don't remember which teacher it was, which kills me. I was having a bad day and I was being the way that most people are, frankly. And the teacher said to me, "Listen, a positive mental attitude will be your key to success." And I don't know why it's stuck in my head, but it did. I have said that to myself 100,000 times. (01:36:48): And today there's one human being in the world who I think is more positive than me, one human being who I've met, who has more positivity than me. I am a relentlessly positive almost, my wife says offensively positive person. She's like, "You know what? Some days you can have a bad day." And I said, "I just don't. Because a positive mental attitude is my key to success." And it's really the way I frame so much of my life, is looking to the positive, looking to the good. And I do it for people whenever I can. And sometimes it frustrates people. But I really believe that most of life is the mindset that you bring to it. And for me in fourth grade, "A positive mental attitude will be your key to success," for some reason, hit me at the right moment in the right way and has stayed with me ever since.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting about that is it's not even like that well, cleverly put. It sounds like a fortune cookie,
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这句话甚至不算特别精妙。听起来像是某种幸运签语，

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You get and you're like, yeah, sure. But I love that that really had so much impact on you, it stuck with you.
turns.zh: 你得到了它，然后你会想，嗯，是啊。但我很高兴它对你影响如此之大，始终萦绕在你心头。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Yeah, I think it was probably timing really. I think I was really having a hard time, and I know at the time two of my friends were not being my friend anymore, and they were my only two friends sort of at the time. And I think I was just open and ready to hear something that I could do to make my life better. And that was the one, and I'm probably predisposed to being an optimist anyway, so it probably landed just right for me.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这可能更多是时机的问题。当时我正深陷困境，而我知道我的两个朋友不再是我的朋友了，他们当时几乎是我仅有的两个朋友。我想我当时心思开放，渴望听到能让生活变得更好的建议。而这句话恰好击中了我的痛点，而且我天生就是个乐观主义者，所以它对我来说简直是量身定制的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A positive mental attitude will be your key to success. Amazing. Final question, maybe just to leave listeners with one tactical thing they can do to become better storytellers. What would that be?
turns.zh: 积极的心态将是你成功的关键。太棒了。最后一个问题，或许能给听众留下一个提升讲故事能力的实用技巧。那会是什么？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: So two things should start every story you ever tell for the rest of your life. So you start with location, where are you? Location activates imagination, right? If I say I'm standing in the kitchen, you've already automatically applied 1000 adjectives to my story. You see the kitchen with great clarity. You probably put me in your own kitchen or your parents' kitchen or a kitchen you see on TV. But if the particularities of the kitchen are relevant to the story, that's what I want you to do. I'm not interested in reproducing locations with some kind of visual accuracy in your brain. I want you to see a fully realized location. So I love location because it's one word that comes imbued with 1000 adjectives. (01:38:59): So you start with location and you start with action, meaning something needs to be happening right away. Literally, I am in a place and I'm doing a thing. It indicates to the audience that you're actually going to tell something that's moving forward. It's why there's a big spaceship shooting of little spaceship in the opening of Star Wars. It's why there's a police officer chasing a guy across a roof. Something is already happening. (01:39:27): We didn't start with nonsense. We started with something happening that grabbed us right away. That's what people want from story. Also, if you're a person unlike me, which is to say anyone who isn't sort of a white straight American man with no physical or mental disabilities, who thinks, I've always thought every room I walk into, I have the right to speak. But if you are unlike me in those regards, you often find, and I know this is true, that it's harder to make space, to get people to hear you if you're from any marginalized or discriminated against group in any way. But what I've been told by women and people of color and members of the LGBTQ community, they've discovered that when I start a story by going, I'm in a place doing a thing, it's a signal to people that I am now telling a story. (01:40:12): And when you can signal to people, I'm now telling a story, they will get quiet for you and they will afford you the opportunity to speak. I didn't know this was going to be the case, but I have had many, many people who I teach this skill to come back to me and say, "My God, people listen to me." And they've said they think they listen because I tell a good story, but they've told me because I start with that location and action, it just tells people, the movie's on. Nobody talks during the movie. You can eat popcorn, but you're not allowed to talk. It silences the room for you and affords you some space to then start doing the work that a good storyteller does to hold those people's attention. So start every story you ever tell for the rest of your life with those two things, and you're already going to be like 50% better than you were before you heard this.
turns.zh:
接下来，在你余生的所有故事开头，都应该用两个要素来开启。首先是地点——你身处何处？地点能激发想象力，对吧？如果我说我在厨房里，你的脑海中瞬间会自动浮现出无数形容词，清晰地勾勒出厨房的画面。你或许会想象是自己家里的厨房、父母的厨房，或者电视里出现过的厨房。但如果这个厨房的细节与故事相关，那才是我希望你做到的。我不期待你能在脑海中精准还原每个细节，我只希望你能构想出一个生动的场景。所以我热爱地点这个元素，因为它本身就蕴含着千言万语的意境。

（01:38:59）接下来是动作——必须有即刻发生的事件。字面意义上，就是我在某个地点做某件事。这向听众传递了一个信号：故事即将展开。正因如此，《星球大战》开场时会有巨大的太空飞船射击小飞船的场面；警察在屋顶追逐嫌疑人时，也会立刻引发观众的兴趣。动作必须鲜明有力。

（01:39:27）我们绝不能从无关紧要的废话开场。我们要用引人入胜的开场瞬间抓住听众的注意力。这正是人们对故事的期待。当然，如果你和我不同——比如非白人、非异性恋、非美国男性、无身体或精神障碍的人——你会发现，要在边缘化或受歧视的群体中争取发言权，实在困难重重。但据女性、少数族裔和LGBTQ群体告诉我，当我用“我在某个地点做某件事”开场时，听众会意识到我要讲故事了。

（01:40:12）当你向听众传递“我要讲故事了”的信号时，他们会安静下来，给你发言的机会。我之前没想到会这样，但许多接受过我培训的人都反馈：“天哪，人们真的在听我讲话。”他们以为是因为我讲得好，实际上是因为地点和动作的组合瞬间点燃了听众的兴趣，就像看电影时大家都安静下来一样——没人说话，只能吃爆米花。这种沉默为你创造了专注讲述的空间，让听众始终保持专注。用这两个要素开启每个故事，你就能比听完这段教程前进步50%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Well, the hits just keep on coming. Matt, you're much more of a philosopher than I imagined you were when we started this conversation. I learned a ton. I'm really excited for people to learn from you. Where can folks find you online if they want to learn more or continue learning from you and work with you potentially, especially companies? And then finally, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 哇哦。好吧，你真是越说越有深度了。马特，比起我们刚开始聊天时，我对你的认知提升了不少。我学到了很多东西。真希望更多人能从你这里受益。读者如果想了解更多信息，或者继续学习、与你合作，特别是企业方面，该怎么找到你呢？最后，听众如何能为你提供帮助呢？

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Sure. So you can find me at matthewdicks.com or if you're a business oriented person or someone who wants to learn, I also have storyworthymd.com, my initials, MD, and that's where I sort of have courses and online training and things like that. So either place you'll be able to find me and contact me. In a non-self-serving sort of version of your second part of the question, I think if you just tell stories, but more importantly, if you ask people to tell you stories, again, creating that space, listen for people who say things like, oh, something like that happened to me once. What they're really saying is, I wish someone would want to hear what happened to me once. (01:41:59): And so I am always someone who's willing to say, oh, tell me that story. Offer someone five minutes of your time so they can finally speak the thing that they've been waiting to speak to someone. So if you just do that, there's going to be more opportunities for storytelling in the world, and ultimately, perhaps that will funnel down to me where they will want to buy my book or visit my website or take some training with me, but just create space for storytelling. I think that'd be a beautiful thing.
turns.zh: 好的。你可以在matthewdicks.com找到我，如果你是一位商务人士或者想学习的人，我还有storyworthymd.com，我的缩写MD，在那里我提供课程和在线培训之类的服务。无论通过哪个平台，你都能找到我并与我联系。关于你问题的第二部分，我想说如果你只是讲述故事，但更重要的是，如果你鼓励别人向你分享故事，关键在于为他们创造一个倾诉的空间。比如，当有人说"我也曾有过类似的经历"时，他们真正想说的是"我希望有人能听我讲讲这段往事"。（01:41:59）所以我总是乐于说"快讲给我听吧"。给别人五分钟时间，让他们终于能把藏在心底的故事说出来。这样一来，世界上的讲故事机会就会越来越多，最终或许会反馈到我这里，比如他们会想买我的书、访问我的网站或者参加我的培训，但最重要的是，要为讲故事创造空间。我觉得这才是最美好的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. What a beautiful way to end it. Matt, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是完美的收尾。马特，非常感谢你今天的到来。

turns.speaker: Matthew Dicks
turns.en: Thanks so much, Lenny. I really appreciate it.
turns.zh: 非常感谢，莱尼。我真的很感激。
